questions.questionText: When did the Soweto Uprising occur?
questions.explanation: Soweto Uprising began when police opened fire on students protesting Afrikaans-medium education policy.

questions.questionText: Who was Hector Pieterson?
questions.explanation: Hector Pieterson became a symbol of the uprising after being shot while fleeing; his photo became iconic.

questions.questionText: What was the Black Consciousness Movement?
questions.explanation: BCM, led by Steve Biko, challenged psychological effects of apartheid and promoted black self-reliance.

questions.questionText: Who was Steve Biko?

options.text: BCM leader who died in police custody

questions.explanation: Biko was founder of BCM, died from brain damage after being arrested and brutalized by police in 1977.

questions.questionText: What were consumer boycotts?

options.text: Refusal to buy from white-owned businesses

questions.explanation: Consumer boycotts targeted white businesses to pressure government through economic loss.

questions.questionText: What was the state of emergency declared in 1986?

options.text: Emergency powers allowing mass detention without trial

questions.explanation: State of emergency gave security forces unlimited powers, leading to detentions and township violence.

questions.questionText: What was COSATU?

options.text: Congress of South African Trade Unions

questions.explanation: COSATU organized millions of workers in strikes that crippled the economy and supported township protests.

questions.questionText: What triggered the Soweto Uprising?

options.text: Government announcement of Afrikaans as medium of instruction

questions.explanation: Students protested government decree forcing Afrikaans as the language of instruction in black schools.

questions.questionText: How did the 1976 uprising spread beyond Soweto?

options.text: Student protests spread nationwide, evolving into broader uprising

questions.explanation: Protests spread to schools across South Africa, with students clashing with police for months.

questions.questionText: What was the role of UDF (United Democratic Front)?
questions.explanation: UDF united hundreds of organizations under non-racial, anti-apartheid principles, becoming main resistance coalition.

questions.questionText: What was the Six Pointers movement?

options.text: Youth demands for liberation and democracy

questions.explanation: Six Pointers demanded free education, release of political prisoners, and democratic rights.

questions.questionText: How did the government respond to township protests?

options.text: Military force, detentions, and state of emergency

questions.explanation: Government deployed military, killed protesters, detained thousands, and imposed media restrictions.

questions.questionText: What role did churches play in 1980s resistance?

options.text: Provided sanctuary, organized protests, and issued anti-apartheid statements

questions.explanation: Churches like the DRC's opposition wing provided shelter, organized campaigns, and challenged apartheid theologically.

questions.questionText: What was the爆动 ( township uprising) of 1984-1986?

options.text: Mass protests, rent boycotts, and clashes with police

questions.explanation: Protests erupted across townships demanding release of prisoners, scrapping of pass laws, and democratic rights.

questions.questionText: Analyze the impact of the Soweto Uprising on the anti-apartheid struggle.

options.text: Marked turning point, mobilizing youth and international attention

questions.explanation: Soweto shocked the world, made apartheid unsupportable internationally, and energized resistance.

questions.questionText: Evaluate the relationship between BCM and later resistance.

options.text: BCM's psychological liberation ideology inspired mass mobilization
Had no influence on later movements

questions.explanation: BCM's emphasis on black dignity and capability empowered activists and shaped mass mobilization strategies.

questions.questionText: How did township organization evolve during this period?

options.text: Street committees and people's courts replaced government structures

questions.explanation: Residents organized parallel governance through street committees, blockades, and people's courts.

questions.questionText: Analyze the role of international media in the 1980s protests.
questions.explanation: International broadcasting showed police brutality, building foreign public opinion and government pressure.

questions.questionText: Evaluate why the government introduced reforms in the 1980s.

options.text: Mounting internal pressure, economic decline, and international isolation

questions.explanation: Reforms like tricameral parliament were attempts to divide opposition while maintaining white control.

questions.questionText: How did the 1980s struggle set the stage for negotiations?

options.text: Government realized apartheid was unsustainable and entered negotiations
Struggle had no connection to negotiations

questions.explanation: Sustained pressure made apartheid economically ruinous, forcing Botha (and later de Klerk) to negotiate.
